toxicity.notes: Bark latex mildly toxic in large doses. Use under practitioner supervision.

Alstonia Scholaris.preparation: Bark decoction: boil 3g-5g dried bark in 200ml water until reduced to 50ml, filter, drink once daily. Never self-medicate.
Alstonia Scholaris.description: Saptaparni is one of the sacred trees of Ayurveda. Modern research confirms potent antimalarial, antibacterial, and hepatoprotective properties via alkaloid pathways.
contraindications: High doses cause vomiting and cardiac depression
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. I

toxicity.notes: Safe at recommended doses.

Arjun.preparation: Kshirpak: boil 3g-6g bark powder in 100ml milk and 100ml water until only milk remains. Take twice daily. For angina, mix with Guggulu.
Arjun.description: Arjuna is Ayurveda's premier cardiac herb, documented for 3000 years. Multiple clinical trials confirm significant improvement in Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction.
contraindications: Consult cardiologist if on anti-hypertensives or statins
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. II
Journal of the American College of Cardiology (JACC)

toxicity.notes: Fruit and leaves safe for all ages including children.

Bael.preparation: Dried fruit powder 5g-10g with warm water before meals. Fresh leaf juice (5-10ml) with black pepper for diabetes. Ripe pulp sherbet with honey for heat exhaustion.
Bael.description: Bael is a 'Tridoshic' herb that balances Vata and Kapha. Its unripe fruit is highly astringent and effective for chronic dysentery, while ripe fruit acts as a mild laxative.
contraindications: Space 2 hours from thyroid and diabetes medications
Not in excessive doses for prolonged periods
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. III
WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants

toxicity.notes: Safe for long-term use at normal doses. Avoid high therapeutic doses in pregnancy.

Tulsi.native_region: Indian Subcontinent — found in almost every home
Tulsi.preparation: Decoction: boil 10-15 fresh leaves in 250ml water for 10 min. Drink with honey for cough. Chew 5 leaves daily for immunity.
Tulsi.description: The 'Queen of Herbs', Tulsi is an adaptogen that enhances the body's resilience to physical and emotional stress. Clinical trials confirm significant efficacy in metabolic syndrome and psychological stress.
contraindications: Recent or scheduled surgery (7 days prior)
Monitor blood sugar if on insulin
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. II
WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Vol. 2

toxicity.notes: Leaves safe. Avoid inhaling dust from bark or old leaves.

Chinar.preparation: Skin/Eyes: Warm leaf infusion as a compress. Internal: Bark decoction (5g bark boiled in 200ml water) for digestive infections.
Chinar.description: The majestic Chinar of Kashmir is not just cultural but medicinal. Its leaves contain Betulinic acid which has been studied for anti-melanoma and anti-inflammatory activity.
contraindications: Inhaling leaf/bark dust can cause respiratory irritation
Internal bark use should be moderate

toxicity.notes: Completely safe. High fiber fruit.

Guava.preparation: Leaf tea: boil 8-10 fresh leaves in 500ml water until 250ml remains. Drink twice daily for digestive/glucose support. Fruit: eat whole.
Guava.description: Psidium guajava is a source of potent antioxidants. Leaf extracts are clinically proven to inhibit alpha-glucosidase, significantly lowering postprandial glucose.
contraindications: Monitor blood sugar if on diabetes medication
Excessive ripe fruit can cause constipation
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. IV

toxicity.notes: All parts safe. Recommended dose for seeds to avoid over-hypoglycemia.

ayurvedic_uses: Diabetes — suppresses starch to sugar conversion
Jamun.preparation: Seed Powder (Jambu Bija Churna): 1g-3g with water 30 min before meals. Fresh fruit: 10-15 berries during seasonal peak for antioxidants.
Jamun.description: Jamboline is a specific glucoside that prevents the conversion of starch into sugar — a unique mechanism confirmed in endocrine research. It is a cornerstone of Ayurvedic diabetes management.
contraindications: Do not combine with high-dose insulin without monitoring
Avoid on empty stomach to prevent acidity
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. II

toxicity.notes: SEEDS HIGHLY TOXIC. Contains Curcin (similar to Ricin). External use ONLY.

Jatropha.native_region: Tropical Americas, naturalized in Indian wastelands
Jatropha.preparation: EXTERNAL ONLY. Leaf paste applied topically. Latex (one drop) for gum infections. Oil should only be used under expert dermatological guidance.
Jatropha.description: Danti-Beej is a potent medicinal but dangerous plant. Its furanoditerpenes promote wound healing but must never be ingested due to cytotoxic curcin proteins.
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. III

toxicity.notes: Completely safe. Acidic nature can affect tooth enamel.

Lemon.preparation: Immunity/Detox: Half-lemon juice in 200ml lukewarm water every morning. Culinary: Add to final cooked dishes to preserve Vitamin C.
Lemon.description: Jambira is unique as its citric acid, though acidic, has an alkalizing metabolic end-effect on urine pH, making it therapeutic for kidney stone prevention.
contraindications: Undiluted juice erodes enamel — rinse with water after
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. III

toxicity.notes: Leaves and bark safe. Sap may irritate sensitive skin (contact dermatitis).

Mango.preparation: Diabetes Support: soak 5-10 young leaves in 250ml water overnight; drink on empty stomach. Bleeding Gums: decoction of bark as a gargle twice daily.
Mango.description: Amra is one of the five most sacred trees in India. Its polyphenol 'Mangiferin' is a potent antioxidant with documented anti-diabetic and anti-cancer properties.
contraindications: Ripe Fruit: High glycemic index — use caution in diabetes
Sensitive individuals may experience sap-induced dermatitis
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. III

toxicity.notes: Mild hepatotoxicity in high internal doses. Safe for external use.

Neem.native_region: Indian Subcontinent — found in almost every village
Neem.preparation: External: Leaf paste applied 15-20 min. Internal (Adults): 1g-2g powder with water for 2 weeks max. Dental: chew fresh twig end.
Neem.description: Nimba is known as 'Arista' (perfect, complete) and the 'Village Pharmacy'. Over 140 bioactive compounds provide unmatched antibacterial and antifungal efficacy.
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. II
WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants

toxicity.notes: All parts safe for standard use.

Pomegranate.native_region: Persia, cultivated in India for 3000+ years
Pomegranate.preparation: Fresh juice 200ml daily. Peel powder 3g-5g with honey for digestive issues. Root bark decoction as anthelmintic (under supervision).
Pomegranate.description: Dadim is called 'Hridya' (heart-pleasing) in Ayurveda. It has the highest concentration of antioxidants of any common fruit and is clinically proven to reduce arterial plaque.
contraindications: Space 2h from ACE inhibitors and blood pressure medications
High doses of root bark are toxic
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. IV

toxicity.notes: Seeds and oil mildly toxic if ingested in large quantities. External use therapeutic.

Pongamia Pinnata.native_region: Indian Subcontinent — coastal and riverine areas
ayurvedic_uses: Deep skin diseases: Eczema, Vitiligo, Psoriasis
Pongamia Pinnata.preparation: Karanja Oil: Apply pure oil to affected skin areas 2x daily. For sensitive skin, mix 1:1 with pure coconut or sesame oil. Leaf paste: apply to non-healing ulcers.
Pongamia Pinnata.description: Karanja is Ayurveda's 'Dermacare' tree. Its furanoflavones like Karanjin have powerful antimicrobial activity against clinical strains of fungus and bacteria.
contraindications: Do not ingest oil or seeds internally without medical supervision
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. II

toxicity.notes: Leaves and pods completely safe. Root bark internally: avoid.

Moringa.preparation: Leaf powder: 1-2 tsp in warm water or smoothie daily. Fresh leaves: cook as vegetable. Pods: cook in curries.
Moringa.description: Called 'miracle tree' — gram for gram more vitamin C than oranges, more calcium than milk, more iron than spinach. Multiple clinical studies support its anti-hyperglycemic and anti-inflammatory properties.
contraindications: Root bark abortifacient — avoid in pregnancy
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. IV
WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Vol. 4

toxicity.notes: Safe for standard use. May cause drowsiness.

Ashwagandha.native_region: Arid regions of India, Middle East
Ashwagandha.preparation: Churna: 2g-5g root powder in a glass of warm milk with honey at bedtime. Ksheerpak (milk decoction) is preferred for better absorption.
Ashwagandha.description: Ashwagandha is the most powerful 'Rasayana' (rejuvenating) herb in Ayurveda. It is an adaptogen that has been clinically shown to reduce cortisol levels by 30%.
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. I

toxicity.notes: Completely safe. One of the most balanced herbs in Ayurveda.

Giloy.preparation: Decoction (Kadha): Boil 10cm stem in 400ml water until reduced to 100ml. Juice: 20ml fresh stem juice with honey. Satva (Starch extraction): 500mg daily.
Giloy.description: Called 'Amrita' (Divine Nectar), Giloy is a premier Rasayana that balances all three Doshas. It was officially recommended in national health protocols for immune support.
contraindications: Monitor blood sugar if on medication
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. I

toxicity.notes: Compete safety profile. High acidity may affect sensitive teeth.

Amla.preparation: Fresh Fruit: 1-2 daily for systemic health. Juice: 20ml with equal water morning. Powder: 3g-6g with warm water or honey.
Amla.description: Amalaki is the foundation of 'Chyawanprash' and 'Triphala'. It contains unique tannins that preserve Vitamin C potency even after heating, providing superior bio-availability.
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. I
Journal of Clinical Biochemistry and Nutrition

toxicity.notes: Safe. Potential mild GI upset if taken on empty stomach.

Brahmi.preparation: Juice: 10ml fresh juice with 1 tsp ghee/honey. Churna: 1g-3g powder with warm milk. Saraswatharishtam (classical liquid): 15ml twice daily after meals.
Brahmi.description: Brahmi is Ayurveda's primary brain tonic. Clinical trials confirm it improves hippocampal neurogenesis and synaptic communication — significantly enhancing memory in 12 weeks.
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. II

toxicity.notes: Safe for long-term use.

Hibiscus.native_region: Tropical Asia — found in every Indian garden
Hibiscus.preparation: Heart: Steep 3-5 fresh/dried petals in 200ml hot water 5 min. Drink twice daily. Hair: Paste of 10 flowers applied with coconut oil as a mask.
Hibiscus.description: Japa is unique for its cooling effect on blood and heart. Clinical studies show Hibiscus tea is as effective as some low-dose ACE inhibitors for mild hypertension.
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. IV

toxicity.notes: Safe. Standard culinary ingredient.

ayurvedic_uses: Anaemia (Rich in Iron and Folic acid)
Curry Leaf.preparation: Diabetes: Chew 8-10 fresh leaves daily on empty stomach. Hair: Boil leaves in coconut oil until blackened; apply as hair tonic.
Curry Leaf.description: Kadi Patta contains unique carbazole alkaloids like Mahanimbine that protect the liver and lower serum cholesterol through lipid metabolism pathways.
contraindications: Monitor blood sugar if using high doses therapeutically with insulin
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. IV

toxicity.notes: Unripe fruit and seeds can stimulate uterine contractions. Avoid in pregnancy.

Papaya.preparation: Dengue: 30ml fresh leaf juice (extracted from clean, younger leaves) twice daily. Digestion: eat ripe fruit before or with meals.
Papaya.description: Papain enzyme in the fruit assists in breaking down tough protein fibers. The leaf juice is now widely used in clinical medicine for thrombocytopenia in Dengue patients.
contraindications: AVOID LEAVES AND UNRIPE FRUIT IN PREGNANCY
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. V
Journal of the Association of Physicians of India (JAPI)

toxicity.notes: All parts safe. Latex may cause contact allergy in sensitive individuals.

Jackfruit.preparation: Diabetes: Decoction of 5-10 young leaves in 250ml water daily. Fruit: Cook unripe fruit as vegetable for fiber; eat ripe fruit as high-energy food.
Jackfruit.description: Panasa is the world's largest tree-borne fruit. Beyond nutrition, its leaves contain 'Artocarpanone' which shows significant clinical potential for managing postprandial hyperglycemia.
contraindications: Diabetes: monitor sugar levels if using leaf tea regularly
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. VI

toxicity.notes: Safe at standard consumption. High doses may cause caffeine dependency.

Tea.preparation: Infusion: Steep 2g-3g high-quality green tea leaves in 80°C water for 3 min. Drink twice daily without milk/sugar for medicinal benefit.
Tea.description: Shyama-Parni (Tea) is a potent source of L-theanine, which modulates the jittery effects of caffeine into a state of 'calm alertness'. Modern oncology research focuses on EGCG for anti-tumor potential.
contraindications: Pregnancy: limit intake to 2 cups daily
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. VII

toxicity.notes: Completely safe. One of the most ancient medicinal plants in Ayurveda.

Sugarcane.native_region: New Guinea — cultivated in India for 4000+ years
Sugarcane.preparation: Fresh juice: drink 200-300ml daily. Add ginger and lemon for enhanced benefit. Jaggery (unrefined sugarcane): use instead of refined sugar for medicinal cooking.
Sugarcane.description: Sugarcane juice is one of Ayurveda's primary medicines for liver and kidney health. Jaggery (raw sugarcane) retains minerals lost in refined sugar processing.
contraindications: Diabetes: commercial refined sugar harmful, but fresh juice in moderation differs
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Vol. IV
WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants

toxicity.notes: External use safe. Internal use of latex (yellow sap) is a strong laxative.

Aloe Vera.native_region: Arid regions of India and Africa
Aloe Vera.preparation: Gel: Apply fresh leaf gel topically twice daily. Juice: 15-30ml clear inner gel blended with water, morning on empty stomach.
Aloe Vera.description: Ghritkumari is a versatile 'Rasayana' in Ayurveda. It is known for its cooling and regenerating properties on skin and liver.

toxicity.notes: Safe in culinary and medicinal doses.

Turmeric.preparation: Golden Milk: 1/2 tsp powder in 250ml warm milk with pinch of black pepper (enhances curcumin absorption by 2000%).
Turmeric.description: Haridra is the most researched Indian medicinal plant. It is a powerful antioxidant and blood purifier used for millennia in Ayurveda.
references: Herbal Medicine: Biomolecular and Clinical Aspects

toxicity.notes: Safe. High doses may cause mild heartburn.

Ginger.preparation: Tea: 1 inch fresh ginger root sliced in 2 cups boiling water, simmer 10 min. Drink with honey for respiratory issues.
Ginger.description: Called 'Vishwabheshaja' (the Universal Medicine) in Ayurveda. It is the primary herb for stimulating digestion and clearing toxins (Ama).

toxicity.notes: Safe. Avoid pure essential oil on skin without dilution.

Mint.preparation: Infusion: 1 tbsp fresh leaves in 1 cup hot water, steep 5 min. For headache: crush fresh leaves and apply to forehead.
Mint.description: Pudina is a refreshing, cooling herb used in Ayurveda to balance 'Pitta' and 'Kapha'. It stimulates digestion without increasing heat.

toxicity.notes: HIGHLY TOXIC — all parts poisonous. External traditional use only under strict supervision. Never ingest.

Arali.preparation: EXTERNAL USE ONLY under practitioner supervision. Never consumed internally. Toxic compounds present in all plant parts.
Arali.description: Oleander is one of the most toxic plants known. In traditional medicine it is used exclusively externally for skin conditions. Modern medicine uses purified cardiac glycosides derived from it.
contraindications: Keep away from children and animals

toxicity.notes: Safe at recommended doses. One of the most important women's health herbs in Ayurveda.

Ashoka.preparation: Bark decoction: boil 10g dried bark in 400ml water, reduce to 100ml, drink twice daily. Ashokarishta (classical formulation): 15-30ml after meals.
Ashoka.description: Ashoka is Ayurveda's primary herb for women's reproductive health, used for 3000+ years. The name means 'remover of sorrow'. Clinical studies confirm significant efficacy for menorrhagia.
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol IV

toxicity.notes: Fruit completely safe. Leaves and seeds contain persin — avoid feeding to animals.

Avacado.native_region: Central Mexico — now cultivated across South India
Avacado.preparation: Eat half a fresh fruit daily. Leaf tea: steep 3-4 leaves in hot water 5 min for blood sugar support. Seed powder: 1g in water — anti-inflammatory.
Avacado.description: Though not traditionally Indian, avocado has been integrated into modern Ayurvedic nutrition for its exceptional fat profile and antioxidant content. The oleic acid content rivals olive oil.
contraindications: Blood thinners: high Vitamin K content — space by 2 hours
references: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition, 2013

toxicity.notes: Edible shoots safe when cooked. Raw shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides — always cook before eating.

Bamboo.native_region: Tropical and subtropical Asia — widespread across India
ayurvedic_uses: Respiratory conditions — bamboo silica as lung tonic
Bamboo.preparation: Young shoots: boil thoroughly before eating. Tabasheer (bamboo silica): 250-500mg with honey for respiratory complaints. Leaf decoction for fever.
Bamboo.description: Bamboo has been used in Ayurveda for millennia. Tabasheer, the siliceous deposit found in bamboo nodes, is a classical Ayurvedic medicine for respiratory and bone conditions.
contraindications: Raw shoots: cook thoroughly — contain cyanogenic compounds
references: Asian Pacific Journal of Tropical Biomedicine, 2012

toxicity.notes: Completely safe. Used as food and medicine across India.

Basale.native_region: Tropical Africa and Asia — widely grown across India
Basale.preparation: Fresh leaves: eat as vegetable daily. Leaf paste: apply to forehead for headache. Juice: 20ml twice daily for constipation relief.
Basale.description: Malabar spinach is a nutritional powerhouse used as both food and medicine in Ayurveda. Its mucilage content makes it an effective gentle laxative and cooling herb.
contraindications: Kidney stones: oxalate content — limit if prone to oxalate stones

toxicity.notes: Leaf alone is safe. Combined with areca nut and tobacco (paan) is carcinogenic. Medicinal use is leaf only without additives.

Betel.native_region: Southeast Asia — widely cultivated across India
Betel.preparation: Medicinal use: chew 2 fresh leaves without additives after meals. Juice: 10ml with honey for cough. Leaf paste on wounds as antiseptic.
Betel.description: Betel leaf has genuine medicinal properties documented in Ayurveda for 3000 years. The medicinal herb is the leaf alone — not the commercial paan mixture which contains carcinogenic additives.
contraindications: Never combine with areca nut or tobacco — carcinogenic combination

toxicity.notes: Known carcinogen when chewed habitually. Limited traditional medicinal use in controlled doses only under practitioner guidance.

Betel Nut.native_region: South and Southeast Asia — widely grown in Kerala, Karnataka
Betel Nut.preparation: Only under qualified Ayurvedic practitioner guidance. Classical formulations use purified areca in controlled doses. Never chew habitually.
Betel Nut.description: Areca nut has classical Ayurvedic applications as an anthelmintic but is recognised as a group 1 carcinogen by IARC when chewed habitually. Medicinal use requires practitioner supervision.

toxicity.notes: Seeds contain ricin — extremely toxic. Castor OIL is safe and widely used. Never consume raw seeds.

ayurvedic_uses: Joint pain and arthritis — topical oil massage
Castor.preparation: Castor oil laxative: 15-30ml with warm milk at bedtime (single dose). Joint massage: warm castor oil applied and wrapped overnight. Never consume raw seeds.
Castor.description: Eranda is one of Ayurveda's most important herbs. The oil is among the safest and most effective laxatives known. The seeds, however, contain ricin — one of the most toxic natural substances.
contraindications: NEVER eat raw seeds — contain lethal ricin
Pregnancy: castor oil induces labour — avoid
Inflammatory bowel disease: avoid oral use
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I
WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants

toxicity.notes: Safe for all ages. Widely used as food herb and medicine across South India.

Doddapatre.native_region: South and East Africa — widely cultivated across India
Doddapatre.preparation: Fresh leaf juice: squeeze 2-3 leaves, extract 5-10ml juice with honey, give for cough. Leaf tea: boil 5 fresh leaves in 1 cup water. Inhale steam from boiling leaves for congestion.
Doddapatre.description: Doddapatre is one of South India's most beloved home remedies for coughs and colds in children. The camphor-like aroma indicates its high carvacrol content which has proven antimicrobial properties.
contraindications: Safe for children at recommended doses
Avoid in pregnancy in large medicinal amounts

toxicity.notes: Latex is toxic and caustic — avoid eye contact. Medicinal use requires practitioner guidance. External traditional use documented.

Ekka.native_region: South and Southeast Asia — dry regions of India
Ekka.preparation: EXTERNAL ONLY under guidance. Leaf warmed and applied to painful joints. Latex applied carefully for dental pain. Never consume internally without expert guidance.
Ekka.description: Madar is used in tribal and Ayurvedic medicine primarily for external applications. It is sacred in Shaivite traditions. Requires careful handling due to caustic latex.
contraindications: Latex contact with eyes causes severe irritation
Internal use: only under qualified practitioner
references: Asian Pacific Journal of Tropical Medicine, 2011

toxicity.notes: Raw unripe berries toxic. Ripe berries and cooked leaves used medicinally. Use under guidance.

Ganike.preparation: Leaf decoction: boil 10g fresh leaves in 300ml water 10 min, drink 50ml twice daily for liver support. Leaf paste topically for skin inflammation.
Ganike.description: Kakamachi is one of Ayurveda's important liver herbs. The ripe berries are used as food in South India. Modern research confirms hepatoprotective properties.
contraindications: Raw unripe berries: toxic — do not eat

toxicity.notes: Completely safe for all ages.

Gauva.preparation: Leaf tea: boil 8-10 leaves in 1 litre water 10 min. Drink 1 cup 2-3x daily before meals.
Gauva.description: Clinical trials confirm guava leaf tea significantly reduces post-meal blood sugar via alpha-glucosidase inhibition.
contraindications: Monitor blood sugar if on diabetes medication

toxicity.notes: Natural henna safe. Avoid black henna containing PPD — causes severe allergic reactions.

Henna.native_region: North Africa, Middle East, South Asia — cultivated across India
ayurvedic_uses: Headache and migraine relief (paste on soles)
Henna.preparation: Paste for cooling: grind fresh leaves, apply to soles of feet and palms. Hair: prepare paste and apply 1-2 hours before washing. Leaf decoction for skin infections.
Henna.description: Henna is deeply embedded in Indian culture and medicine. Lawsone gives the red-orange dye and is strongly antimicrobial and antifungal. The cooling effect on soles is documented in Ayurvedic texts.
contraindications: G6PD deficiency: lawsone can trigger haemolysis

toxicity.notes: Seeds and oil mildly toxic internally. External skin application safe and well-documented.

Honge.preparation: Oil: apply to affected skin twice daily. Leaf paste on wounds. Mix 1:4 with sesame oil for sensitive skin.
Honge.description: Karanja oil is a classical Ayurvedic treatment for skin diseases. Same species as Pongamia Pinnata — regional name variant.
contraindications: Do not ingest seeds or oil

toxicity.notes: Safe for general use. Monitor blood sugar if on diabetes medication.

Insulin.native_region: Central America — widely cultivated in South India for diabetes
ayurvedic_uses: Type-2 diabetes management — most researched use
Insulin.preparation: Fresh leaf: chew 1-2 fresh leaves on empty stomach daily. Juice: blend 2 leaves in water, strain, drink 30ml morning and evening. Most effective consumed fresh.
Insulin.description: Called 'insulin plant' because leaves actively lower blood glucose. Widely grown in South Indian home gardens specifically for diabetes management. Clinical studies confirm significant hypoglycaemic effect.
contraindications: Diabetes medication: synergistic effect — may cause hypoglycaemia — monitor closely
Adjust medication doses with practitioner if using regularly
references: Journal of Clinical and Diagnostic Research, 2014

toxicity.notes: Completely safe. Widely used in food, medicine and ritual.

Jasmine.native_region: South and Southeast Asia — cultivated across India
Jasmine.preparation: Flower tea: steep 8-10 fresh flowers in hot water 5 min. Drink 1-2 cups daily. Flower paste on forehead for headache. Jasmine oil for scalp and skin massage.
Jasmine.description: Jasmine is deeply integrated into Indian culture, medicine and religion. The scent alone has documented anxiolytic effects. Used in Ayurveda for Pitta-related conditions including heat, inflammation and anxiety.
contraindications: Essential oil: dilute before skin application
Pregnancy: jasmine oil may stimulate contractions in large amounts

toxicity.notes: Safe at recommended Ayurvedic doses.

Nagadali.native_region: Sri Lanka, South India — moist evergreen forests
Nagadali.preparation: Flower powder: 1-3g with ghee twice daily. Seed oil: apply topically for skin conditions. Classical formulation Nagakesara Churna available commercially.
Nagadali.description: Nagakesara is a highly valued classical Ayurvedic herb mentioned extensively in Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita for bleeding disorders and skin conditions.
references: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol III

toxicity.notes: Contains powerful alkaloids. Safe at traditional doses. Internal use only under practitioner supervision.

Nithyapushpa.preparation: Leaf tea: 3-4 leaves in 1 cup hot water, drink 1 cup daily for blood sugar. Flower garland/paste for headache. Never exceed recommended dose.
Nithyapushpa.description: Periwinkle gave medicine vincristine and vinblastine — two of the most important cancer chemotherapy drugs. The plant itself has traditional use for diabetes and hypertension in many cultures.
contraindications: Do not self-medicate at high doses

toxicity.notes: Safe for general use. High potassium — caution in kidney disease.

Nooni.native_region: Southeast Asia, Pacific Islands — grown in coastal South India
Nooni.preparation: Noni juice: 30ml on empty stomach morning and evening. Fruit: eat 1-2 ripe fruits daily. Leaf decoction for external wounds.
Nooni.description: Noni has been used in Pacific and South Asian traditional medicine for 2000+ years. Modern research is exploring its significant antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties.

toxicity.notes: Safe at Ayurvedic doses. Protected species in India — use only sustainably sourced material.

Raktachandini.native_region: Eastern Ghats, South India — endemic to Andhra Pradesh
Raktachandini.preparation: Wood paste: grind red sandalwood with water, apply to skin for inflammation and cooling. Decoction: 3-5g powder in 200ml water, boil 10 min, drink for fever.
Raktachandini.description: Rakta Chandan is a highly prized Ayurvedic herb with powerful anti-inflammatory and skin-benefiting properties. It is an endangered species protected under Indian wildlife law.

toxicity.notes: Completely safe. One of the gentlest medicinal plants.

Rose.native_region: Central Asia — cultivated across India especially Rajasthan
Rose.preparation: Rose water: use as eye wash and facial toner. Gulkand (rose petal preserve): 1-2 tsp daily as cooling tonic. Rose tea: steep dried petals in hot water 5 min.
Rose.description: Rose is central to both Ayurvedic and Unani medicine as a cooling, heart-opening herb for Pitta constitution. Gulkand (rose petal jam) is a classical formulation for digestive heat.
contraindications: Ensure pesticide-free flowers for medicinal use
Rose hip seeds: mild laxative in large amounts

toxicity.notes: Fruit completely safe. Seeds have mild sedative properties — do not consume large amounts.

Sapota.native_region: Mexico and Central America — widely cultivated across India
Sapota.preparation: Fresh ripe fruit: eat 1-2 daily. Bark decoction: fever and diarrhoea treatment in traditional medicine. Leaf tea: anti-inflammatory.
Sapota.description: Sapota is rich in natural sugars, minerals and antioxidants. In Ayurveda it is used as a nutritive tonic especially for weakness and digestive disorders.
contraindications: Diabetes: high natural sugar — monitor intake
Seeds: mild sedative — do not eat large quantities
references: Journal of Food Science and Technology, 2015

toxicity.notes: High oxalic acid content. Safe in small culinary amounts. Avoid large medicinal doses if prone to kidney stones.

Wood Sorel.native_region: Widespread across India — common in gardens and roadsides
Wood Sorel.preparation: Fresh leaves: add small amounts to food as souring agent. Leaf juice: 10ml with water for digestive complaints. Paste on skin for infections.
Wood Sorel.description: Changeri is mentioned in Charaka Samhita as a digestive herb. Its sour taste makes it a traditional culinary medicine for stimulating digestion and appetite.
contraindications: Kidney stones: high oxalate — avoid if prone
